content:
The image shows two corn ears on the same stalk. The lower ear has a large, irregular dark brown-black mass of spore material at its base/tip, with the husk pulled back revealing what appears to be a massive smut gall replacing part of the ear. The gall has a dark, powdery/dusty brown appearance consistent with teliospore masses. The upper ear appears mostly normal with orange kernels visible.

Key observations:
- Large dark brown gall/spore mass at the ear (not a mold growing over kernels, but a gall replacing ear tissue)
- The mass appears to have ruptured, releasing dark brown spores
- The affected ear appears deformed/replaced by the gall structure
- This is localized to the ear, not the tassel

Comparing to candidates:
- **Common_Smut**: Galls on ears, stalks, leaves, or tassels; initially white/silvery tissue, later dark spore masses. This matches well.
- **Head_Smut**: Replaces entire ears or tassels with smut galls; teardrop-shaped ears lacking silks; plants systemically infected. Head smut typically replaces the entire ear/tassel and causes plant dwarfing.

The gall here is large and localized to one ear while the other ear appears normal — this is more consistent with Common Smut, which produces discrete galls on individual plant parts rather than systemic infection of the whole plant. The dark brown powdery spore mass bursting from the ear is classic common smut.
